sentences.text:
Dated this the 04th day of December, 2025 The petitioner is the 2nd accused in C.C.No.36/2021 on the file of the Court of the Judicial First Class Magistrate-III, Kannur, ('Trial Court', in short), which originates from Crime No.522/2020 registered by the Chakkarakkallu Police Station, Kannur,
alleging the commission of the offences punishable under Sections 406, 420 and 120B read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

sentences.text:
.
2. The prosecution allegation, in brief, is that:

sentences.text: Between 20.11.2017 to 02.01.2018, the accused 1 and 2, in furtherance of their common intention, had hatched a conspiracy, to cheat the 4 th respondent (defacto complainant) had received Rs.4,00,000/- from the 4 th respondent by bank transfer to their bank accounts, on the assurance of a job to the post of Junior Assistant in the Regional Co-operative Milk Producers Union Ltd, a public CRL.MC NO. 11025 OF 2025 4 2025:KER:93766 sector undertaking.

entities.text: Regional Co-operative Milk Producers Union Ltd
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: However, the accused failed to secure the employment and refused to return the money.
Thus, the accused persons have committed the above offences.
3. I have heard the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.

4. The learned counsel for the petitioner submits that, even if the allegations in Annexure A2 First Information Report and Annexure A3 Final Report are taken on their face value, the same will not constitute the offences charged against the petitioner.
It was the 1 st accused who received the consideration from the defacto complainant, which is evident from the statement of the witness appended in Annexure A3 Final Report.
The petitioner has no culpability in the crime.
Even if the petitioner faces the trial, the same will not lead to a conviction.
Hence, the entire proceedings, as against the petitioner, may be quashed.
5. The learned Public Prosecutor opposes the Crl.M.C.
He submits that there are specific overt acts 2025:KER:93766 levelled against the petitioner.
The petitioner and the 1 st accused had jointly received Rs.4,00,000/- from the 4 th respondent assuring him a job in the Regional Co- operative Milk Producers Union Ltd.

entities.text: Regional Co- operative Milk Producers Union Ltd.
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: The Investigating Officer has laid the Final Report on 31.10.2021.
It is after four years that the petitioner has filed this Crl.M.C, without any plausible explanation for the delay, and when the case is posted for trial.
There is no merits in the Crl.M.C.
Hence, the Crl.M.C may be dismissed.
6. The specific case of the prosecution is that, the petitioner and the 1st accused had hatched a conspiracy to cheat the 4th respondent.

They in furtherance of their common intention, received money from the 4th respondent, which was transferred to the bank accounts of both the accused, on the assurance of the securing an employment in a public sector undertaking.
7. I have carefully gone through the allegations in Annexure A3 Final Report, wherein there are specific overt acts attributed against the petitioner.

It is well-established that this Court has broad plenary powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which corresponds to Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita,

sentences.text: However, such inherent power, though expansive in nature, is not unbridled or unlimited.
They are to be exercised sparingly, with circumspection, and within the parameters delineated by judicial precedents.

One of the elementary principles to quash a criminal proceeding is that, even if allegations in the first information report or the complaint are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, the same will not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused.

(Read the decisions in State of Haryana and others v. Bhajan Lal and others [(1992) Supp (1) SCC 335], Central Bureau of Investigation v. Aryan Singh and Others [(2023) 18 SCC 399], Daxaben v. State of Gujarat and Others [(2022) 16 SCC 117] and CRL.MC NO. 11025 OF 2025 7 2025:KER:93766 Monica Kumar and Another v. State of U.P. and Others [(2008) 8 SCC 781]).

sentences.text: 9. The Hon'ble Supreme Court has also consistently cautioned that High Courts, while exercising jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code, should not embark upon a "minitrial" or weigh the sufficiency of evidence, which falls within the domain of the Trial Court.
The scope of enquiry is confined to whether, on a plain reading of the FIR/complaint and accompanying material, the ingredients of the alleged offence are disclosed.

(Read the decisions in Rajiv Thapar and others v.
Madal Lal Kapoor [(2013) 3 SCC 330] and HMT Watches Ltd. v. Abida M.A. and another [(2015) 11 SCC 776]).
10.

Madal Lal Kapoor [(2013) 3 SCC 330]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In Muskan v. Ishaan Khan (Sataniya) [2025 KHC 6914], the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that the inherent power under Section 482 of the Code is extraordinary, but must be exercised sparingly.

It is the duty of the High Court to intervene where continuation of criminal proceedings would amount to an abuse of process 2025:KER:93766 of law, or where the dispute is purely of a civil nature and criminal colour has been artificially given to it.
Conversely, where disputed questions of fact arise requiring adjudication, the matter must ordinarily proceed to trial.

11. It is also trite that though no statutory period of limitation is prescribed under Section 582 of BNSS/482 Cr.P.C., the litigant seeking to quash a proceeding must approach the Court within a reasonable time period; if not, he must convincingly address the reasons for the delay.

At any rate,
the litigant cannot approach this Court at his whim and caprice, merely because no period of limitation is prescribed in the statute.
In such cases, the High Court can decline to exercise its inherent jurisdiction.

After bestowing my anxious consideration to the facts and the materials on record, particularly after going through the specific overt acts attributed against the petitioner in Annexure A3 Final Report,
and if the allegations are taken on their face value, they prima facie 2025:KER:93766 attract the offences, I am not satisfied that this is a fit case to exercise the inherent powers of this Court under Section 528 of the BNSS to quash all further proceedings in C.C.No.36/2021.
The Crl.M.C is devoid of any merits and is only liable to be dismissed.
Nonetheless, the Trial Court is directed to consider and dispose of the above case, in accordance with law, untrammelled by any observation made in this order.
